newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - July 7.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - July 7.

text.p: This daily press summary is produced for Reuters by the Broadcast Monitoring Company, which is responsible for its contents. DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- LATE INVESTORS COULD FACE FINES

A City committee has proposed that investors who sell their shares and post their certificates late should be fined 5 pounds stg a day. The suggestion is that brokers should collect the fines from clients. The City has been given until the end of the month to comment on the recommendation, which has come from a committee that includes representatives of the leading institutional and private client stockbrokers and registrars.
-- LLOYD'S FACES MORE LOSSES, SAY ANALYSTS

Chatset, a company that analyses syndicate performance, has warned that Lloyd's of London is hitting the downturn of the insurance cycle and is about to plunge into losses again. The analysts claim that marine underwriters are being tempted to reinsure heavily following of a steep drop in premium ratings. However, according to Charles Sturge of Chatset, there is evidence of greater care being taken this time, with underwriters reinsuring outside Lloyd's.
-- OLD COMPUTERS IN VAT TRAP

Changes announced in last week's summer Budget mean that it is now more financially expedient for companies to smash up their large computers rather than sell them on the second-hand market. Sellers of computers costing more than 50,000 pounds stg will now have to pay punitive amounts of VAT if they sell on the computer before the end of its working life. In some cases, according to Graeme Ross of accountants KPMG, sellers could be liable to pay more in VAT disposals than the selling price.
THE TIMES
-- WATERSTONES THINKS SMALL

Book retailer Waterstones is to launch a 10m stg investment programme that will see 50 smaller size stores opened over the next five years. The programme is part of a strategy aimed at making the chain, owned by WH Smith, into Britain's leading book chain with 150 branches.
-- MEMORY FOCUSES ON TAIWAN VENTURE

Scots microchip systems producer Memory Corporation is to engage in a joint venture with a Taiwanese computer producer in a bid to break into the digital camera market. Memory Corp is expected to make sales of 5.6m stg next year through the deal with Hsin Lin Computer Co. The move is part of attempts by new chief executive David Savage to turn round Memory's 2m stg loss last year by using its technology in new markets.
-- SAFEWAY EXTENDS SCANNERS

Supermarket chain Safeway will on Monday launch a 'smart' scanner that greets customers by name when they use an in-store loyalty card. The device features a screen detailing how many points are on the card, the last three items scanned, and a running total for the trip. The card will make use of an extensive database Safeway has compiled on its customers tastes and preferences using old loyalty card till receipts.
THE GUARDIAN
-- MURDOCH ROW SPLITS BSKYB

Directors at satellite broadcaster BSkyB have reacted angrily to comments from Rupert Murdoch that shares in the company had been heavily overvalued. Murdoch was quoted in an unsigned article in the Sunday Times, a paper owned by his News Corporation, commenting on the recent slump in BSkyB's share price. The media magnate, who owns 40 per cent of BSkyB, shrugged off the decline in the company's share price in recent weeks from almost 700p to 444p by claiming the stock had been 'grossly overpriced'.
-- FRENCH CLEAR EUROTUNNEL

A French judicial inquiry has cleared Eurotunnel, the Anglo-French operator of the Channel Tunnel, of any responsibility for the fire which badly damaged a section of the tunnel last November. The findings of the inquiry have yet to be made public, but Eurotunnel chairman Patrick Ponsolle told the Europe 1 radio station on Sunday that the inquiry had already shown that Eurotunnel's installations and systems were not to blame.
-- BROWN PRESSES FOR SHOP FLOOR STAKEHOLDERS

Chancellor Gordon Brown has ordered a fundamental inquiry into the practicalities of introducing democracy into the workplace and offering staff the opportunity to influence company strategy. The move to offer workers a stake in the long-term future of their companies is part of efforts by Brown to introduce a new workplace culture designed to enhance industrial relations and to increase companies' performance.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- 100M STG SHOCK FOR NATIONAL POWER AS JUDGE RE-OPENS HEARING

A High Court judge has taken the almost unprecedented step of convening a further hearing into the case of electricity companies removing surplus cash from their pension funds. The reopening of the case follows a ruling from the same judge last month that the use of pension surpluses by National Power and National Grid to help fund redundancy programmes was legal. Solicitors representing National Power pensioners went to the judge last week claiming to have discovered a flaw in his original ruling.
-- RAILTRACK QUIZZED OVER 46M STG 'WEATHER PROVISION'

Rail regulator John Swift has asked Railtrack, the operator of Britain's rail infrastructure, to explain a 46m stg provision made in the company's accounts for 'severe weather and other matters'. Swift is reported to have asked Railtrack to provide a detailed breakdown of the provision. There have been suggestions that the provision may have been intended to help keep Railtrack's profits down to avoid confrontation with the government.
-- WINDFALLS AND PROPERTY DEMAND PROVIDE SHOT IN ARM FOR DIY SALES

A new report from retail consultants Verdict Research has predicted that the market for DIY products will surge over the next two years, boosted by building society windfalls and a buoyant housing market. According to the report, the value of DIY spending last year reached its highest level since the boom years of the 1980s, with the total market worth some 10.9bn stg.
